chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: Not getting copies of her records or being paid
summary: She had to buy her own copy, sent copies home to Pittsburgh, never knew a side was released, and doubts she was paid.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Yes, but you felt the title in your mind is "Gone With The Wind?"

Yes.
It came up because I -- as I said before -- I had just come to New York. I don't think I'd been in New York two months when that was made.
And I came to New York from Pittsburgh.
So the club that I was working in, I sent about ten copies back to Pittsburgh.
And I got a note that it was number one on their hit parade down there.

So, can we assume from what you say, that it wasn't a practice for record companies to make copies of the records available to the performers when they were issued? Because I do believe that "Stop, You're Breaking My Heart" did come out.

No, I mean --
In fact, I didn't even know that it was ever released. And, of course, "Gone With The Wind" -- on the other side of "Gone With The Wind" was

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Jimmy Farrell's vocal of 'Harbor Lights.' See, I wasn't on both sides.
And the copy that I had, I had to go out and buy. Yes. Maybe they give away some now, but in those days, not particularly.
How about other economic considerations. You know how much they paid you and what the terms --
I don't know if I even got paid for that recording. The only one I remember getting paid for was the next one. You know, the one when I did 'Loch Lomond.'
I didn't even get paid for that.
